The People of the Iliad and the Odyssey

Every named mortal who takes part in the action of the two poems: where Homer says they came from, their families as Homer gives them, every line that names them, who killed whom, and how many lines each of them speaks.

Where they came from

Each person is placed at the home Homer gives them at the time of the action: for the Iliad, the place they came to Troy from; for the Odyssey, the place where they live. Captives are placed at their own homes (Briseis at Lyrnessus), and exiles at the home they came from (Patroclus at Phthia, with Opoeis noted). Where Homer names only a people, the person is placed with that people's home and marked as inferred. Dashed rings mark a region whose town is not known; an asterisk marks a modern identification of a Homeric place.

Drag to move, double-click or use + to zoom. Click a place for the people from it, and a name for that person's card.

Who speaks

Lines of direct speech, counted from the DICES database of epic speeches and checked against the text. Direct lines are spoken in the poem's own scenes. Embedded lines are quoted inside another character's narration — the term narratologists use (Irene de Jong); the character who narrates is a secondary narrator. When Odysseus tells his wanderings, the words of Polyphemus, Circe or Tiresias that he quotes count for them, not for him, so nothing is counted twice. Lines in Odysseus' lying tales are counted but marked.

Families, as Homer gives them

Every statement of kinship in the two poems, and nothing from later sources. A patronymic counts as a statement of fatherhood. Each link carries the lines where Homer states it; gods are in italics.

Method and data

Compiled for Iosif Lazaridis from the Greek text of Homer (Monro–Allen, via Perseus), with Murray's Loeb translation, the Perseus treebank, the DICES database of epic speeches and the Pleiades gazetteer. Built 12 October 2026.
